notes.title: Linux Fundamentals & Kernel Basics
notes.content: Understanding the core components and philosophy of Linux
concepts: Linux Kernel - manages hardware and system resources
Unix Philosophy - do one thing and do it well
System Calls - interface between user programs and kernel
Daemon processes - background system services
POSIX compliance - portable operating system interface
terminology: kernel: The core of the OS managing hardware/resources
shell: Command interpreter (bash, zsh, sh)
daemon: Background process running without user interaction
process: Running instance of a program with unique ID (PID)
environment variables: Named values accessible to programs
tty: Terminal device representing a user connection
inode: Data structure storing file metadata
superuser/root: User with unrestricted system access (UID 0)
keyCommands: top - monitor system resources in real-time
uptime - show how long system has been running

notes.title: Linux Boot Process
notes.content: Understanding BIOS/UEFI, bootloader, and system initialization
concepts: BIOS/UEFI - firmware that initializes hardware
MBR/GPT - partition tables for disk organization
Bootloader - loads kernel into memory (GRUB, systemd-boot)
Kernel initialization - detects hardware, mounts root filesystem
Init system - first process (PID 1) managing services
terminology: BIOS: Basic Input/Output System - legacy firmware
UEFI: Unified Extensible Firmware Interface - modern firmware replacement
MBR: Master Boot Record - legacy boot sector
GPT: GUID Partition Table - modern partitioning scheme
GRUB: GRand Unified Bootloader - common Linux bootloader
multiboot: Ability to choose OS at boot time
runlevel: Numeric representation of system state (0-6)
systemd: Modern init system for service management

notes.title: Shell Fundamentals & Environment
notes.content: Shells, commands, variables, and command expansion
concepts: Shells - interpreters that process user commands
Bash vs other shells - feature differences and compatibility
Command structure - command, arguments, options, redirection
Environment variables - configuration values for processes
Command substitution & expansion - parameter expansion, globbing
Quoting & escaping - controlling special character interpretation
terminology: shell: Command interpreter processing user input
bash: Bourne Again Shell - most common Linux shell
prompt: Text displayed waiting for user input
built-in: Command executed internally by shell (not external)
alias: Shorthand for frequently used commands
variable: Named storage for values
glob: Pattern matching with *, ?, [ ]
escape: Using backslash to prevent special meaning
keyCommands: echo - display text or variable values
export - make variable available to child processes
source/. - execute commands from file in current shell
type - show command type (built-in, alias, etc)

notes.title: Linux Filesystem Hierarchy
notes.content: Directory structure and Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS)
concepts: FHS - standardized directory organization
Root filesystem - essential system files
bin vs sbin - user vs system binaries
Various /etc directories - configurations
/var data - dynamic data: logs, spool, cache
/proc and /sys - kernel information interfaces
terminology: FHS: Filesystem Hierarchy Standard
root directory (/): Top-level directory
inode: File metadata structure
hard link: Multiple names for same inode
symbolic link: Pointer to another file/directory
mounting: Attaching filesystem to directory tree
partition: Division of storage device
volume: Mounted storage containing files
keyCommands: df - show disk space usage by filesystem
du - show disk usage of files/directories

notes.title: File Permissions & Links
notes.content: Understanding Unix permissions model and file linking
concepts: Permission bits - read (4), write (2), execute (1)
User-Group-Other model - rwx permissions for each
Special permissions - setuid, setgid, sticky bit
Hard links - shared inode references
Symbolic links - pathname-based pointers
Permission inheritance - defaults and umask
terminology: permissions: Access control for files/directories
rwx: read (r=4), write (w=2), execute (x=1) bits
umask: Default permissions mask for new files
setuid: Execute with file owner privileges
setgid: Execute with group privileges or inherit directory GID
sticky bit: Only owner can delete file in directory
hard link: Multiple directory entries sharing same inode
symlink/soft link: File containing path to another file

notes.title: Managing Files & Directories
concepts: File copying - cp with recursion and force options
Moving/renaming - mv preserves ownership and permissions
Safe deletion - rm caution and recovery considerations
Directory operations - mkdir with parents, rmdir
Globbing patterns - wildcards for multiple files
File searching - find with various criteria
terminology: recursive: Applies operation to directory and all contents
force: Override protection settings without prompting
preserve: Keep original file attributes when copying
target: Destination file or directory
source: File or directory being copied/moved
pattern: String with wildcards for matching multiple files
criteria: Selection conditions for find command
predicate: Test condition in find expressions
keyCommands: locate - find files by name in database

notes.title: Filesystem Administration
concepts: Partitioning - dividing disks into sections
Filesystem types - ext4, XFS, Btrfs, NTFS
Creating filesystems - mkfs and formatting
Mounting/unmounting - attaching to directory tree
Automatic mounting - /etc/fstab configuration
Filesystem checking - fsck and recovery tools
terminology: partition: Logical division of storage device
filesystem: Organization of files and metadata on storage
mount point: Directory where filesystem is attached
fstab: File Stab - table of filesystems to mount at boot
device node: File representing hardware (e.g., /dev/sda1)
journaling: Recording changes before committing to prevent corruption
UUID: Universally Unique Identifier for persistent device naming
fsck: Filesystem check tool for finding and fixing issues

notes.title: User & Group Administration
notes.content: Managing user accounts and group membership
concepts: User accounts - local authentication and system accounts
UID/GID - numeric identifiers for users and groups
Password management - /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow encryption
Group membership - primary and supplementary groups
User creation/deletion - useradd, userdel commands
Home directories - user login environment setup
terminology: UID: User Identifier - numeric ID for user
GID: Group Identifier - numeric ID for group
passwd: Password file storing user account info
shadow: Shadow password file storing encrypted passwords
primary group: Default group for user's files
supplementary group: Additional group memberships
skeleton: Template files copied to new home directory
sudoers: File controlling sudo privilege escalation
keyCommands: id - show user and group info

notes.title: Sudo & Privilege Escalation
notes.content: Granting elevated privileges safely and securely
concepts: Principle of least privilege - minimal required permissions
sudo mechanism - temporary privilege escalation with logging
sudoers file - configuration for sudo access control
visudo - safe editor for /etc/sudoers
Logging sudo activity - security auditing and accountability
Alternatives to sudo - su command and setuid
terminology: privilege escalation: Gaining higher-level access
sudo: SuperUser DO - run command as another user
sudoers: File controlling who can use sudo
visudo: Safe editor validating sudoers syntax
nopass: Allow command without password prompt
policy: Set of sudo rules for specific user/group
audit log: Record of who ran what command when
su: Switch User - change to different user account
keyCommands: sudo - execute command with elevated privileges
sudo -u user - run as specific user
su username - switch to specific user

notes.title: System Initialization & Runlevels
notes.content: Init systems, systemd, and service management
concepts: Init system - first process managing all others
Traditional runlevels - 0-6 system states
systemd - modern replacement with service units
Service activation - manual, on-demand, automatic
Service dependencies - controlling startup order
Logging - journald system logging in systemd
terminology: init: First process (PID 1) managing system services
runlevel: Numeric system state 0-6
systemd: Modern init system using unit files
unit: systemd configuration for service/mount/etc
target: systemd grouping of units (like runlevels)
socket activation: Starting service on access
journald: Systemd journal logging daemon
cgroup: Control group for resource limiting
